title: Cholesterol & Bile Acids Metabolism
objectives: Describe bile acid synthesis pathways and enterohepatic circulation
Explain the roles of cholesterol and bile acids in lipid digestion and absorption
Analyze clinical disorders related to cholesterol and bile acid metabolism
Identify pharmacological targets in these pathways

overview.title: Cholesterol Fundamentals
overview.content:
Cholesterol is an essential structural component of cell membranes and precursor for steroid hormones, bile acids, and vitamin D. The body maintains tight regulation of cholesterol homeostasis through de novo synthesis (mainly liver), dietary absorption, and excretion (as bile acids).

Key Functions

  • Membrane Integrity: Modulates fluidity and raft formation
  • Precursor Molecule: For bile acids, steroid hormones, vitamin D
  • Lipoprotein Core: Structural component of LDL/HDL particles

Cholesterol Properties

Structure

  • 27-carbon steroid nucleus
  • Hydroxyl group at C3
  • Double bond at C5-C6
  • 8-carbon side chain at C17

Characteristics

  • Amphipathic (polar OH + hydrophobic rings)
  • Insoluble in water (requires lipoproteins)
  • ~140g total body content (1.5g turnover/day)

cholesterol_synthesis.title: Cholesterol Biosynthesis
cholesterol_synthesis.content:
Mevalonate Pathway

Location: Cytoplasm and ER (liver, intestine, adrenal)

Key Enzymes: HMG-CoA reductase (rate-limiting), squalene synthase

Synthetic Steps

  1. 3 Acetyl-CoA → HMG-CoA (thiolase & HMG-CoA synthase)
  2. HMG-CoA → Mevalonate (HMG-CoA reductase, NADPH)
  3. Mevalonate → Isoprenoids (IPP/DMAPP)
  4. 6 Isoprenoids → Squalene (30C)
  5. Squalene → Lanosterol (cyclization)
  6. Lanosterol → Cholesterol (19 additional steps)

Regulation

Transcriptional: SREBP-2 activation when cholesterol low

Post-translational: HMG-CoA reductase phosphorylation (AMPK)

Feedback: Oxysterols accelerate enzyme degradation

bile_acid_metabolism.title: Bile Acid Synthesis & Circulation
bile_acid_metabolism.content:
Primary Bile Acids

Synthesis: Liver (0.5g/day), via classic (neutral) and alternative (acidic) pathways

Products: Cholic acid (CA) and chenodeoxycholic acid (CDCA)

Key Reactions

  1. Cholesterol → 7α-hydroxycholesterol (CYP7A1, rate-limiting)
  2. Side-chain oxidation/cleavage (CYP27A1)
  3. Conjugation (glycine/taurine) → bile salts

Enterohepatic Circulation

Process: 95% reabsorbed in ileum (ASBT transporter)

Secondary BAs: Bacterial dehydroxylation → DCA & LCA

transport_regulation.title: Transport & Homeostasis
transport_regulation.content:
Cholesterol Transport

  • LDL: Delivers cholesterol to peripheral tissues (ApoB-100)
  • HDL: Reverse cholesterol transport (ApoA-I)
  • NPC1L1: Intestinal cholesterol absorption

Bile Acid Transporters

  • NTCP: Hepatic uptake of conjugated bile salts
  • BSEP: Canalicular secretion of bile acids
  • OSTα/β: Basolateral efflux

Regulatory Nodes

  • FXR: Bile acid-activated nuclear receptor
  • LXR: Oxysterol-activated cholesterol sensor
  • FGF19: Ileal hormone that suppresses CYP7A1

clinical_correlations.title: Clinical Correlations
clinical_correlations.content:
Cholesterol Disorders

  • FH: LDL receptor mutations → ↑LDL (xanthomas)
  • Smith-Lemli-Opitz: DHCR7 deficiency → low cholesterol

Bile Acid Disorders

  • Cholestasis: BSEP mutations (PFIC2)
  • Gallstones: Cholesterol supersaturation
  • BA malabsorption: Diarrhea (FXR agonists treat)

Therapeutics

  • Statins: HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors
  • Ezetimibe: NPC1L1 inhibitor
  • Bile acid sequestrants: Cholestyramine
  • FXR agonists: Obeticholic acid (PBC)

faqs.title: FAQs
faqs.content:
Why does cholesterol synthesis require so much NADPH?+
Each cholesterol molecule requires 18 ATP and 26 NADPH equivalents, reflecting the energy cost of reducing saturated hydrocarbon chains from acetyl-CoA precursors.
How do bile acids emulsify dietary fats?+
Their amphipathic structure (polar hydroxyl/COO- and nonpolar steroid rings) allows formation of micelles that solubilize lipids for pancreatic lipase action.
Why are bile acids conjugated with glycine/taurine?+
Conjugation lowers pKa, preventing protonation in acidic duodenum and maintaining solubility for efficient intestinal reabsorption.
What causes the genetic defect in familial hypercholesterolemia?+
Mutations in LDL receptor (Type IIa), ApoB (Type IIb), or PCSK9 (gain-of-function) impair LDL clearance, causing severe premature atherosclerosis.
